title: Pick a realtime transport for each feature
purpose: Decide between periodic polling, long polling, Server-Sent Events and WebSockets for four product features: a notification feed, a stock ticker, a chat and a collaborative cursor.
summary: Two questions pick a realtime transport: who sends the data, and how much delay is acceptable. Polling asks on a timer, long polling holds the request open, Server-Sent Events stream text from the server, and WebSockets carry messages both ways. Four deep dives apply the questions to a notification feed, a stock ticker, a chat and a collaborative cursor.
explanation: Persistent connections remove the time a message waits for the next poll, but they do not make packets travel faster. Pick the simplest transport that matches the direction of the data.

learning_check.question: A notification feed only pushes short text events from the server. Which transport fits best, and why not WebSockets?
learning_check.answer: Server-Sent Events: the data goes one way and is text, and the browser reconnects automatically. WebSockets also work, but the application must then build its own reconnects and state handling.

slides.heading: Which transport fits each feature?
slides.notes: State the decision: four features, four transports, and two questions to choose between them.

visual.subtitle: Polling, long polling, SSE or WebSockets

slides.heading: Four ways to get live data
slides.notes: Reveal one transport at a time. Ask who opens the connection and who can send on it.

items: Polling: the client asks again on a timer
Long polling: the server holds the request until an update
SSE: one long HTTP response streams text from the server
WebSockets: both sides send messages at any time

slides.heading: What a persistent connection removes
slides.notes: With polling, a ready message waits for the next request. SSE and WebSockets send it at once. The packet travel time stays the same.

left.label: Periodic polling
items: Message waits for the next poll
Empty checks still cost a request

right.label: SSE or WebSockets
items: Server sends when data is ready
Travel time is unchanged

visual.verdict: Low latency here means no queuing delay.

slides.heading: Short intervals cost bandwidth
slides.notes: Ten thousand clients poll and get no new messages; each empty check is about 850 bytes. At 60 seconds the server receives 1.13 megabits per second; at 1 second, over 60.

slides.heading: Only the server sends
slides.notes: Open a deep dive for a feature where updates flow from the server to the browser only. Previous returns here.

items: Notification feed: short text events
Stock ticker: many updates per second

slides.heading: Both sides send
slides.notes: Open a deep dive for a feature where the browser also sends data at any time. Previous returns here.

items: Chat: users send and receive messages
Collaborative cursor: positions flow both ways

slides.heading: How to decide
slides.notes: Turn the deep dives into a repeatable procedure for any new feature.

items: Both sides send at any time: WebSockets
Server sends text only: SSE
Delay is fine and updates are many: poll
No SSE support in the client: long polling

slides.heading: Feed: Server-Sent Events
slides.notes: The feed is one-way text, which is what SSE was designed for. The browser parses events and reconnects for you.

items: Server streams text/event-stream on one response
Browser fires a DOM event per message
On a drop, the browser reconnects and sends the last ID
For an image, send a link; fetch it over HTTP

slides.heading: Ticker: push or batch?
slides.notes: If every price must arrive at once, use SSE. If the screen may lag, periodic polling batches many updates into one response.

left.label: SSE
items: Each price arrives when ready
One long-lived connection

right.label: Periodic polling
items: One response holds many updates
Fewer requests, saves battery

visual.verdict: At high rates, long polling sends the most requests.

slides.heading: Chat: WebSockets
slides.notes: Both people send at any time, so the client must send after the handshake, which SSE cannot do. WebSockets can, with small frames.

items: Messages go both ways on one connection
Each frame adds only 2 to 14 bytes
The app builds its own reconnects and state
Long polling is the older fallback

slides.heading: Cursor: small messages over WebSockets
slides.notes: Many small position updates flow both ways. One large queued message delays every message behind it, so keep messages small.

items: Send small position messages both ways
A large queued message blocks the ones behind it
Split large messages into chunks
Watch bufferedAmount before you send
